#15 Perhaps you have something different but related in mind:

Stone–Čech compactification does admit a double-dual description using the interval, if the second dual consists of suitable algebra homomorphisms, as in Marra & Reggio 2016 §3:

β(X)  ≃  Hom⁡MV(C(X,I),I) , \beta(X) \;\simeq\; \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{MV}}\big(C(X,I),I\big) \mathrlap{\,,} β(X)≃HomMV​(C(X,I),I),

where the hom-set is of “MV-algebras” and equipped with the topology of pointwise convergence.

So in spirit this looks like a double-dualization monad construction, but it’s not quite.

#17 To reiterate, the Stone-Cech compactification of the point is the point, β(∗)=∗\beta(\ast) = \astβ(∗)=∗. That immediately rules out your proposal.

You are proposing [X,Y]≔Cp(X,Y)[X,Y] \coloneqq C_p(X,Y)[X,Y]:=Cp​(X,Y). But this still gives ∗↦[[∗,I],I]≃Cp(I,I)\ast \mapsto \big[ [\ast,I],I\big] \simeq C_p(I,I)∗↦[[∗,I],I]≃Cp​(I,I), which disagrees with the Stone-Cech compactification ∗↦β(∗)=∗\ast \mapsto \beta(\ast)=\ast∗↦β(∗)=∗.

On your proposed restricted Yoneda argument, cf. Theorem 2.6 on p. 550 of Isbell’s Adequate subcategories. This says explicitly:

A 1-cell is not right adequate for compact spaces.

Here “1-cell” means an arc like our interval III, and “right adequate” means codense. So this says that the restricted Yoneda functor for the full subcategory consisting of III is not fully faithful. Isbell gives counter examples on the next couple of pages.

Finally, the codensity construction for the full subcategory {I}\{I\}{I} must retain naturality with respect to every continuous endomorphism u:I→Iu:I\to Iu:I→I: its functionals satisfy Φ(u∘f)=u(Φ(f))\Phi(u\circ f)=u\big(\Phi(f)\big)Φ(u∘f)=u(Φ(f)). This is a different condition from continuity of Φ:Cp(X,I)→I\Phi:C_p(X,I)\to IΦ:Cp​(X,I)→I, which defines the internal double dual. So even a successful codensity calculation would need a separate justification for identifying its result with that internal double dual. But the point-example above shows that your proposed identification cannot hold.

First, Nat(IX,I)\mathrm{Nat}(I^X, I)Nat(IX,I) is not the internal double dual of Def. \ref{TheContinuationMonad}. It is the codensity monad of the one-object subcategory {I}\{I\}{I}. For the internal hom, the point-example stands.

Second, the Lemma is false. The step “This forces J=evaJ = \mathrm{ev}_aJ=eva​” does not follow. Naturality gives that J(f)∈f(A)J(f) \in f(A)J(f)∈f(A), hence J(f)=f(af)J(f) = f(a_f)J(f)=f(af​) for some afa_faf​, but this afa_faf​ may depend on fff. The power maps x↦xnx \mapsto x^nx↦xn add nothing, since they are among the ϕ\phiϕ already assumed.

Isbell’s counterexample is at the end of p. 551. His “left transformation from a point PPP to a 2-cell SSS over a 1-cell III” is exactly a natural J ⁣:C(S,I)→IJ \colon C(S,I) \to IJ:C(S,I)→I. Let SSS be a triangle with sides aba bab, aca cac, bcb cbc. For h ⁣:S→Ih \colon S \to Ih:S→I, let J(h)J(h)J(h) be the unique xxx such that some connected component of h−1(x)h^{-1}(x)h−1(x) meets all three sides. Uniqueness is by the Jordan curve theorem; for existence see p. 552.

This JJJ is natural: if KKK is such a component for hhh, then KKK lies in a component of (ϕ∘h)−1(ϕ(x))(\phi \circ h)^{-1}\big(\phi(x)\big)(ϕ∘h)−1(ϕ(x)), which therefore also meets all three sides, so J(ϕ∘h)=ϕ(J(h))J(\phi \circ h) = \phi\big(J(h)\big)J(ϕ∘h)=ϕ(J(h)). In particular J(hn)=J(h)nJ(h^n) = J(h)^nJ(hn)=J(h)n.

But JJJ is not an evaluation. For p∈Sp \in Sp∈S, let hhh be the rescaled distance from ppp. Then h−1(h(p))={p}h^{-1}\big(h(p)\big) = \{p\}h−1(h(p))={p} meets at most two sides, so J(h)≠h(p)J(h) \neq h(p)J(h)=h(p). Since the 2-cell is compact Hausdorff, the question of what Isbell means by “compact” does not arise.

On the closure question: Nat(IX,I)\mathrm{Nat}(I^X,I)Nat(IX,I) is the closed subspace of IC(X,I)I^{C(X,I)}IC(X,I) cut out by the equations Φ(ϕ∘f)=ϕ(Φ(f))\Phi(\phi \circ f) = \phi\big(\Phi(f)\big)Φ(ϕ∘f)=ϕ(Φ(f)). (It is this equalizer, not IC(X,I)I^{C(X,I)}IC(X,I) itself, that is the cone.) It contains the image of XXX, hence contains βX\beta XβX. Equality for all XXX is equivalent to your Lemma, and so it fails at X=SX = SX=S.

What is true is the first clause of Isbell’s Thm. 2.6: the 2-cell I×II \times II×I is codense in compact spaces. There, naturality includes binary operations such as (x,y)↦(xy,0)(x,y) \mapsto (x y, 0)(x,y)↦(xy,0), which make JJJ a ring homomorphism. Hence β\betaβ is the codensity monad of {I×I}↪Top\{I \times I\} \hookrightarrow {\mathrm{Top}}{I×I}↪Top.

But that is not a continuation monad either, so I suggest removing this example here, or moving it to codensity monad with I×II \times II×I in place of III.
